title: Reproducible cluster headache remission following SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccination: a case report
abstract: Cluster headache (CH) is among the most severe primary pain disorders and can be highly refractory to conventional treatment. Although SARS-CoV-2 infection and mRNA vaccination have been predominantly linked to the exacerbation or new onset of CH, we here report the case of a 26-year-old male with a seven-year history of refractory chronic CH (cCH) who experienced a rapid and sustained complete remission (CR) following SARS-CoV-2 mRNA booster vaccination. This remission, documented by daily pain intensity ratings on a numerical rating scale (NRS, 0–10) derived from a prospectively maintained headache diary, was characterized by an abrupt cessation of high-intensity nocturnal attacks immediately following vaccination. After sustained remission of the previous chronic nightly attack pattern, the patient subsequently developed recurrent CH activity; a subsequent JN.1-adapted mRNA vaccination was again followed by rapid remission. The repeated close temporal association between vaccination and remission is notable, although spontaneous disease fluctuation cannot be excluded in a single-patient observation. To characterize the immunological environment accompanying clinical remission, we performed longitudinal multiparametric immunophenotyping of peripheral blood at three time points surrounding the 2025 vaccination event. We observed a transient expansion of natural killer (NK) cells and monocytes, upregulation of the checkpoint marker PD-1 on CD4+ T cells, and expansion of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), observed in temporal association with the onset of CR. Antigen-specific stimulation assays revealed a concurrent induction of IFN-γ and TNF-α producing CD4+ T cells, consistent with a TH1-polarized immune response. To our knowledge, this is the first report of a reproducible, vaccination-induced CR in chronic CH, supported by high-resolution clinical and immunological longitudinal data. The findings suggest that targeted immune activation may be capable of resetting pathological neuro-immune circuits in refractory headache disorders and warrant prospective investigation.

title: Documented SARS-CoV-2 infection and risk of neurodegenerative disease diagnosis: a target trial emulation across three real-world cohorts
abstract: Electronic health record studies have reported increased incidence of Neurodegenerative Diseases (NDD) following SARS-CoV-2 infection, but causal interpretation is complicated by differences between infected and uninfected individuals, differential follow-up, incomplete infection ascertainment and competing mortality. We emulated target trials using Danish national health registries, the US TriNetX network, and UK Biobank data, including individuals aged \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\ge $$\end{document}70 years without a previous diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, or unspecified dementia. Historical pre-pandemic and contemporary test-negative control designs were evaluated. Cause-specific cumulative incidence functions were estimated using cross-fitted targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE), accounting for measured baseline confounding, dependent censoring, and death as a competing event. We estimated marginal effects for the diagnoses of Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, unspecified dementia, and a composite endpoint, and explored heterogeneity among clinically relevant subgroups. Across cohorts, control-group designs, outcomes, and follow-up horizons, documented SARS-CoV-2 infection was not associated with a consistent increase in average risk for NDD diagnosis. Exploratory analyses nevertheless suggested higher risks among older individuals and among those with established dementia-related risk factors, including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, depression, and hearing impairment. These patterns were observed across several analyses, although their magnitude and consistency varied between cohorts and outcomes, and require further confirmation in independent studies.

Similar content being viewed by others Introduction Recent studies suggest that Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2(SARS-CoV-2) infections are associated with short-term alterations in brain structure1,2 and biomarkers of Neurodegenerative Disease(NDDs)3,4. However, so far there is no clear evidence that these short-term alterations causally trigger a clinical manifestation of NDDs. Recent meta-analyses5,6,7 suggest an increased risk of new-onset NDDs, including all-cause dementia8,9,10,11,12,13, Alzheimer’s Disease (AD)8,14,15,16, vascular dementia17, and Parkinson’s Disease (PD)15,16,18. Most of this evidence is derived from retrospective analyses of Electronic Health Record (EHRs), administrative health data, or other routinely collected data sources. Although such datasets provide the scale and follow-up required to investigate relatively rare and slowly developing outcomes, their use for causal inference is complicated by several sources of bias. A central challenge is the definition of an appropriate comparison group. Individuals with and without a documented SARS-CoV-2 infection may differ systematically in demographic characteristics, comorbidities, healthcare use, and probability of being tested. Testing policies and infection ascertainment also changed substantially over the course of the pandemic. During the early pandemic, testing was often concentrated among high-risk populations, including residents of long-term care facilities and individuals with severe symptoms, whereas many infections in the general population remained undetected. Consequently, comparisons between individuals with documented infection and controls that are either untested or test-negative may be affected by both baseline confounding and selection into testing and diagnosis. Furthermore, many known risk factors for dementia19 and PD20 are also discussed in the literature as risk factors for Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) morbidity: older age21, sex21, pre-existing comorbidities (e.g., diabetes21, cardiovascular diseases21, obesity21, hypertension21, depression22), smoking behavior21, sleep disturbances23, and local air pollution24. Demographic features such as education, income status, and ethnicity can also be assumed to play a role due to the effects on potential exposure to SARS-CoV-2 and inequality in healthcare utilization25. Previous studies have commonly addressed these differences using propensity score matching based on a subset of measured covariates9,10,11,13,14,17,18. However, matching alone may not eliminate bias if the propensity model is misspecified. Moreover, causal interpretation requires explicit consideration of the assumptions under which effects are identifiable from observational data. Longitudinal follow-up introduces additional challenges. Individuals with documented infection may have different observation periods from controls because infections occurred during different stages of the pandemic and because healthcare contact patterns changed over time. Differential loss to follow-up may therefore induce censoring bias when it is related to both measured patient characteristics and subsequent disease risk. Death is also an important competing event, particularly in older populations. Many risk factors for NDDs are associated with COVID-related and all-cause mortality, and death may preclude a diagnosis that would otherwise have occurred. Analyses that do not account appropriately for censoring and competing mortality may therefore yield biased estimates of cumulative disease risk. We conducted a multi-cohort causal analysis to estimate the effect of documented COVID infection on the cumulative incidence of AD, PD, unspecified dementia, and a composite (NDD) endpoint. We analysed three large observational data sources representing distinct healthcare systems, data-generating processes, and infection-ascertainment settings: Danish national health registries, the US TriNetX network, and the UK Biobank. Depending on the cohort and pandemic wave, follow-up extended to five years. This design allowed us to assess whether conclusions were consistent across national registry data, routinely collected US healthcare data, and a prospective population cohort. To address limitations of previous observational studies, we emulated target trials using both historical pre-pandemic controls and contemporary test-negative controls. We estimated marginal effects using cross-fitted Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation (TMLE) estimation for time-to-event outcomes with competing risks, jointly accounting for measured baseline confounding, dependent censoring, and death as a competing event. We evaluated the plausibility of the assumptions required for causal interpretation using overlap diagnostics, alternative control-group designs, and sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding. In addition to estimating population-average effects, we explored effect heterogeneity according to age and established risk factors for NDD. Methods Cohorts We employed three large-scale real-world datasets from Denmark, the USA and the UK for our study. Danish cohort The Danish cohort was based on data from several different Danish registries. Citizens in Denmark have a personal ID number which is used to track all encounters with the public health system and other authorities. Utilizing this, we linked and extracted information from the following sources: the Danish National Patient Registry covering all hospital inpatient and outpatient encounters in Denmark since 1994, the Register of Pharmaceutical Sales with all prescriptions dispensed from a Danish pharmacy since 1994, COVID surveillance test data containing all SARS-CoV-2-tests (PCR and antigen) taken in Denmark since 2020, the Danish Vaccination Registry with all COVID vaccinations in Denmark since 2020, and the Danish Central Person Registry with demographic information on everybody living in Denmark since 1968. The administrative censoring date for all registries was the 17th of November 2024, which allowed targeting effects after 1500 days in the first, 1300 days in the second and 1100 days in the third wave. All data were pseudonymized and kept in a secure, certified compute environment. TriNetX cohort TriNetX is a global federated network for real-world data and analytics26. The network consists of EHR–derived real‐world data that includes more than 220 healthcare organizations across 30 countries. TriNetX aggregates de‐identified patient‐level data contributed by participating healthcare organizations, with data remaining locally hosted under a conservative security and governance model. Data domains include demographics, diagnoses, procedures, medications, encounters, laboratory results, and oncology‐specific and genomic data. All data are harmonized to the TriNetX common data model using standardized clinical terminologies to ensure cross‐site comparability. The data used was specifically compiled for this study on May 15, 2025 and consists of 2,999,997 patients from 64 healthcare organizations that are part of the Dataworks - USA network, including both in- and outpatient encounters. Administrative censoring was set for April 30, 2025, which made effect targeting after 1700 days possible for confirmed first-wave COVID cases, 1500 days for second-wave, and 1300 days for third-wave cases. All analyses were run on the Lucid Analytics platform. UK Biobank The UK Biobank is a large-scale population study comprising health and lifestyle information from around 500,000 participants in the UK, enrolled at ages from 40 to 69 between 2006 and 201027. During an initial assessment center visit, participants underwent health measurements and questionnaires. This data is linked to their health records from hospitals (inpatient only) and general practitioners, which document diagnoses over time. The administrative censoring date for the hospital inpatient records is October 31, 2022 for England, August 31, 2022 for Scotland, and May 31, 2022 for Wales. In general, this restricted the follow-up analysis to 700 days after the first wave. General practitioner health records, largely complete only until 2017, were excluded from this study. Target trial protocol Target trial emulation potentially allows the estimation of the effect that some exposure has on an outcome even if the exposure is not randomized28. A challenge in this regard is that the infection status of a SARS-CoV-2 infected person may not be documented. For that reason we only focused on people with a documented positive test result. Further key components of the emulated target trial, including eligibility criteria, exposure strategies, start of follow-up (index date), end of follow-up, outcomes, causal contrasts, and analysis plan are summarized in Table 1. In short, analyses were run for multiple NDD endpoints characterized by the first documented diagnosis with specific International Classification of Diseases Version 10 (ICD-10) codes and their sub-classifications: AD (G30), PD (G20), unspecified dementia (F03), and a composite endpoint summarizing all three. In the Danish cohort, we allowed the AD endpoint to be additionally defined by prescriptions of antidementiva, and the PD endpoint by anti-Parkinson drugs or dopamine agonists in the Registry of Pharmacy Sales (see Supplementary Table S1 for exact Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classification codes). A single diagnosis (or drug) code was sufficient to flag an incident NDD case. Patients who were diagnosed with any NDD not covered by the three ICD-10 codes were retained in the analysis, as additional comorbidities do not make later diagnoses of G30, G20 or F03 impossible in the spirit of a competing event. For the COVID group, the index date was the date of the first reported infection with SARS-CoV-2; depending on the experiment either by a positive antigen / PCR test or a hospital diagnosis. The whole available follow-up period up to the administrative censoring date of each cohort was used. Unlike subjects with a reported SARS-CoV-2 infection, control subjects do not have an index date that is directly apparent in the data. We tested two control group designs with different strategies to fix the index date, both of which have benefits and drawbacks. - Pre-pandemic control follow-up (historical controls) The first strategy involved creating a control pool with follow-up before the COVID pandemic. For each COVID patient, a control subject was selected and the control index date set to a date on which the control was the same age as the COVID at the time of infection. The control’s follow-up duration was matched to that of another sampled COVID patient, but truncated at December 31, 2019, if it extended into 2020 or beyond. This was done to ensure that control patients were never infected during the analysis period. This “pre-pandemic control follow-up” strategy is illustrated in the upper portion of Fig. 1. An advantage of this design is that it rules out undetected COVID infections in the control group because the virus did not yet exist during the analysis period. However, it is possible that additional (potentially unquantifiable) confounding was introduced due to the time gap between the case and control groups. For example, the lockdowns imposed during the pandemic may have had lasting impacts on patients’ mental health and neurological condition, potentially with independent effects on NDD diagnosis frequencies. There may also be changes in the healthcare systems that became effective over time. Finally, the hard truncation before 2020 introduces administrative censoring. - Tested positive vs. negative (contemporary controls) The second strategy, illustrated in the bottom half of Fig. 1, included only subjects tested for COVID. Controls were patients tested during the same period as the COVID group, but always negative (then and every other time their test results were reported). To align the groups’ index date distributions as closely as possible, control index dates were directly sampled from the COVID group index date distribution (regardless of the controls’ actual test dates), and all available follow-up until the administrative censoring date was included. The “tested positive vs. negative” strategy for COVID studies offers advantages over pre-pandemic control follow-up by eliminating time gaps and related distribution shifts between case and control analysis periods. This design thus ensures that control groups, comprising individuals who tested negative during the same pandemic phase, are inherently similar to the COVID positive group. For instance, if early testing limitations restricted testing to high-risk individuals, both groups would reflect this situation similarly. However, the “tested positive vs. negative” approach has also notable limitations: it neglects individuals with unreported infection status (both positive and negative) and is influenced by the diagnostic accuracy of COVID tests at the time of application, potentially leading to an inconsistent exposure status variable. Furthermore, this control group design excludes infections diagnosed through clinical or hospital settings. Our chosen approach to control index date sampling also may introduce immortal time bias because the controls are guaranteed to survive between the index date and the first reported test in a considered period. However, this bias is not expected to be large and should be sufficiently addressed by modeling death as a competing risk. We only included individuals who were at least 70 years of age on the index date and did not have a prior diagnosis of AD, PD or unspecified dementia. Patients with were excluded because NDD diagnoses within the first month were likely chance discoveries when patients saw a doctor for their COVID infection (possible surveillance bias). Table 2 summarizes key demographics per cohort, infection wave, and COVID or control group. As expected, age differences between the COVID positive and control groups were insignificant for all datasets. The Danish cohort had the highest counts of EHR entries, and fewer entries were present in the UK Biobank on average. For the “tested positive vs. negative” design, Supplementary Table S2 additionally shows how often the “tested positive” and “tested negative” groups got actually tested during each wave. Across cohorts, we found a difference in mean test frequencies between the COVID and control group, albeit with large standard deviations. On average, COVID patients were tested a bit more often, which is possibly due to repeated testing once an infection had been detected. Table 3 provides an overview of sample sizes for the different cohorts and experiments with the composite endpoint (see Supplementary Tables S3-S5 for AD, PD and unspecified dementia endpoints). To address the computational challenges of emulating the target trial with raw control groups, particularly convergence issues with TMLE, we sampled three times the number of COVID patients from the control group and then performed 1:1 propensity score matching. Beyond runtime considerations, combinations of matching and TMLE have been found to exhibit favorable effects on bias reduction in causal effect estimation29. Propensity scores were estimated via a HistGradientBoostingClassifier30 using hyperparameters optimized in a grid search and covariates specified in Table 4; more detailed information on field identifiers for the used features can be found in Supplementary Table S1. A caliper width of 0.2 times the standard deviations of the propensity score logits in the control pool was used in the matching step. A small pre-study on the UK Biobank revealed that both the percentage of COVID patients who get successfully matched and also the estimate of Risk Ratio (RRs) from propensity matching alone may depend a lot on the chosen caliper width for the “pre-pandemic control follow-up” design, but not for “tested positive vs. negative” (Supplementary Figure S1). Propensity score matching followed by TMLE, on the other hand, was a lot more robust against different caliper widths. title: COVID‐19 nucleic acid vaccines, their many virtues, some deficiencies and unsuspected novel features. A reflection after pandemic resolution and present endemic SARS-CoV-2 circulation
abstract: In the successful fight against COVID-19, there is little doubt that vaccines made with RNA or vectored-DNA have played a major role. However, their benefits are somewhat shadowed by their insufficiencies in fighting the viral infection, its transmission and, consequently, the lack of robust herd protection. Moreover, a few rare but significant side effects have caused some community worries. The main aim of this commentary is to provide a critical reflection on the above issues. We will also discuss some other nonspecific effects of these vaccines, potentially enlarging the spectrum of vaccination benefits but also involving intriguing inflammatory patterns in need of special consideration.

title: Pediatric Immunoglobulin A (IgA) Vasculitis Temporally Associated With Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2): Clinical Characteristics, Renal Involvement, and Short-Term Outcomes
abstract: Background: Immunoglobulin A vasculitis (IgAV) is the most common systemic vasculitis in children.Data describing IgAV temporally associated with severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) in geographically underrepresented populations remain limited.Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 32 children with IgAV temporally associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection or exposure evaluated from March 2022 to March 2025.Renal involvement was defined as documented hematuria and/or proteinuria.Evidence of SARS-CoV-2 comprised polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-confirmed infection, documented close contact, or IgG seropositivity.The infection-to-onset interval was calculated only for PCR-confirmed cases.Comparisons by renal involvement used the Mann-Whitney U and Fisher's exact tests and were considered exploratory.Results: Median age was 4.0 years (interquartile range (IQR), 2.0-9.0);17 (53.1%)were female children.PCRconfirmed infection was documented in 20 (62.5%), with a median infection-to-onset or presentation interval of 61.0 days (IQR, 31.0-89.3).All children had palpable purpura; 22 (68.8%) had abdominal pain, 10 (31.3%) had arthralgia or arthritis, and 11 (34.4%) had renal involvement.Children with renal involvement had longer hospital stays (median 4.0 vs. 3.0 days; nominal p = 0.023) and higher neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratios (median 2.5 vs. 1.3; nominal p = 0.041).Corticosteroids were given to 25 children (78.1%), although indications were not consistently recorded.Resolution of the initial episode was documented in all children; four (12.5%) experienced relapse.Conclusions: The clinical features of IgAV temporally associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection or exposure were broadly consistent with childhood IgAV, with renal involvement in approximately one-third of patients.Associations with hospitalization duration and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio were exploratory.Small sample size, retrospective design, heterogeneous ascertainment of SARS-CoV-2 exposure, and limited standardized follow-up restrict interpretation; causality cannot be inferred.

title: Comparative Transcriptomic Analysis of Gene Expression Patterns in Neutrophils from Rheumatoid Arthritis and COVID-19
abstract: Abstract Background Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disorder characterised by chronic inflammation and immune dysregulation, and neutrophils play a key role in its progression. COVID-19 also involves neutrophil hyperactivation that contributes to severe immune responses. Emerging evidence links COVID-19 to increased incidence or exacerbation of RA, potentially through overlapping immune mechanisms. Objective To compare neutrophil transcriptomic profiles in RA and COVID-19 and identify shared immune pathways and disease-specific features. Methods Publicly available neutrophil RNA-seq count data from the Gene Expression Omnibus were analysed: RA versus healthy controls (GSE116899) and COVID-19 versus healthy controls (GSE212041). A second COVID-19 comparison (severe versus convalescent) was assembled from GSE272381 and GSE227116. Differential expression was analysed with DESeq2, pathway enrichment with fgsea (Hallmark gene sets) and topGO (Gene Ontology biological process and molecular function). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were compared between diseases by direction of change. Results In RA neutrophils, 11,355 DEGs were identified, of which 90 had an absolute log2 fold change of at least 2 with p<0.05 (70 upregulated, 20 downregulated). Twenty-four Hallmark gene sets were positively enriched at adjusted p<0.05, led by interferon alpha and interferon gamma responses, and Gene Ontology analysis highlighted type I interferon, antiviral and double-stranded RNA terms. In COVID-19 neutrophils, 420 DEGs were identified (37 upregulated, 383 downregulated), and no Hallmark gene set reached adjusted p<0.05. Of the 90 RA DEGs, 46 changed in the same direction in COVID-19 without reaching significance, and 27 changed significantly in the opposite direction, including CAMK1G, SIGLEC1, OAS1 and OAS3. In the second COVID-19 comparison, several of these genes, including OAS1, OAS3 and SIGLEC1, changed in the same direction as in RA. Conclusions RA neutrophils show a transcriptional programme enriched for interferon and antiviral-response pathways. Part of the RA signature is shared with COVID-19 neutrophils, while a subset of genes diverges, and this divergence depended on the COVID-19 comparison used. These findings are hypothesis-generating and provide candidate genes for experimental validation.

title: Pentosan polysulfate sodium limits pulmonary inflammation in a SARS-CoV-2 mouse model
abstract: ABSTRACT Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection remains prevalent globally, causing severe pulmonary inflammation and mortality in up to 10% of patients. While the introduction of effective vaccines has substantially reduced the number of severe coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) cases, there are currently few available therapeutics that have been developed. Pentosan polysulfate sodium (PPS) has been shown to possess potent anti-inflammatory activity in influenza infection and allergen-induced rhinitis models and was recently demonstrated to inhibit SARS-CoV-2 infection in vitro . As such, we hypothesized that PPS may represent an attractive therapeutic that could be utilized for SARS-CoV-2 infection and COVID-19. Using the K18-hACE2 mouse model of SARS-CoV-2 infection, we administered PPS (6 mg/kg) from either 1 (early) or 3 (late) days post-infection via intranasal instillation and then examined the efficacy in mitigating viral-induced inflammation and severe disease outcomes. We found that the early administration of PPS was accompanied by significant improvements in weight loss, clinical disease presentation, and neutrophilic airway inflammation. Early PPS administration also significantly reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production at both the mRNA and protein levels while having no impact on viral titers or interferon and antiviral gene expression. Histologically, early treatment significantly prevented severe pulmonary inflammation and tissue remodeling. Comparatively, late administration of PPS worsened weight loss and clinical disease presentation following SARS-CoV-2 infection. Moreover, late administration was unable to prevent significant increases in pro-inflammatory cytokines and was further associated with significantly downregulated antiviral-associated genes. Histological examination also showed no protection in the late PPS administered groups. Taken together, these findings underscore the significance of time-dependent administration and demonstrate the therapeutic potential of PPS for treatment of SARS-CoV-2-induced inflammation. IMPORTANCE Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) continues to cause infections globally, with most cases resulting in mild to moderate disease outcomes. However, approximately 10% of patients experience virally induced hyperinflammation leading to poor outcomes. As such, new or repurposed therapeutics need to be rapidly implemented to address this urgent medical need. Here, we show that pentosan polysulfate sodium (PPS) is a leading Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved therapeutic that significantly mitigates SARS-CoV-2-induced pulmonary inflammation. Critically, timing of PPS during the infection establishment and progression is critical for PPS efficacy, highlighting time-dependent responses that must be considered for further human clinical implementation. The findings from this study demonstrate that PPS holds significant promise as a repurposed anti-inflammatory agent for SARS-CoV-2 infection.

source_records.abstract: ABSTRACT Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection remains prevalent globally, causing severe pulmonary inflammation and mortality in up to 10% of patients. While the introduction of effective vaccines has substantially reduced the number of severe coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) cases, there are currently few available therapeutics that have been developed. Pentosan polysulfate sodium (PPS) has been shown to possess potent anti-inflammatory activity in influenza infection and allergen-induced rhinitis models and was recently demonstrated to inhibit SARS-CoV-2 infection in vitro . title: Serologic and clinical correlates of within-host SARS-CoV-2 genetic diversity in a large acute-infection cohort
abstract: Within-host evolution of SARS-CoV-2 has been described primarily in the setting of prolonged infection among immunocompromised individuals, but the determinants of viral genetic diversity during acute infection remain incompletely understood. In particular, the relationships among prior immune exposure, vaccination, viral burden, and intra-host viral populations early in infection remain unclear. We examined whether serologic markers of prior immune exposure or vaccination were associated with within-host SARS-CoV-2 genetic diversity during acute infection. We analyzed SARS-CoV-2 whole-genome deep sequencing data from nasal swabs collected at the time of diagnosis from 4200 acutely infected individuals enrolled across a geographically diverse cohort. Intra-host viral genetic diversity was quantified as the number of intra-host single nucleotide variants (iSNVs) detected per sample. Host immune and clinical factors evaluated included receptor-binding domain (RBD)-neutralizing antibody positivity, nucleocapsid antibody positivity, Spike IgG antibody positivity, vaccination status, and immunosuppressed status. Associations between these factors and viral diversity were assessed using multivariable Poisson generalized linear models with a log link, adjustment for overdispersion, an offset for callable genome size, and covariates retained in the base model. At least two iSNVs were detected in viruses from 1977 (47%) participants, indicating measurable within-host genetic diversity during acute infection. RBD-neutralizing antibodies were detected in plasma from 1,598 (38%) participants. In multivariable analyses, RBD-neutralizing antibody positivity was independently associated with higher iSNV counts ( p < 0.001; incidence rate ratio [IRR]=1.24, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.10–1.41). Similar associations were observed for nucleocapsid antibody positivity ( p < 0.001; IRR = 1.27, 95% CI 1.12–1.44). In contrast, vaccination status, defined as receipt of at least one dose, was associated with lower iSNV counts ( p = 0.043; IRR = 0.86, 95% CI 0.74–1.00), while immunosuppressed status was not significantly associated with iSNV counts ( p = 0.23). Additional factors associated with higher iSNV counts included lower viral loads in nasal mucosa, lower plasma N antigen levels, and longer duration of symptoms prior to diagnosis. Because samples were collected at a single timepoint, these associations do not establish whether antibody positivity contributes to within-host diversity or instead reflects infection timing or prior immune exposure. Serologic markers of prior immune exposure and any-dose vaccination status were associated with measurable differences in intra-host SARS-CoV-2 genetic diversity during acute infection in this large cohort. These findings provide a large descriptive baseline for future longitudinal studies of within-host viral dynamics. Four studies from which we obtained the samples have been registered in ClinicalTrials.gov: ITAC, ID: NCT04546581, Date: 2020–09–08; TICO, ID: NCT04501978, Date: 2020–08–03; TESICO, ID: NCT04843761, Date: 2021–04–09 and ICOS, ID: NCT04385251, Date: 2020–05–08.

title: Psychological resilience among emergency medical staff during the COVID-19 pandemic in Taizhou, China
abstract: Objective During the COVID-19 pandemic, emergency medical staff faced unprecedented occupational stressors, making psychological resilience a critical protective resource. This study aimed to identify the factors related to psychological resilience among emergency medical staff during the COVID-19 pandemic in Taizhou, China. Methods In April 2022, we surveyed 69 medical staff from four medical systems at different levels in Taizhou City, Zhejiang Province, using a convenience sampling method. The survey incorporated scales for psychological resilience, job engagement briefs, perceived social support, and the Simple Coping Style Questionnaire. Results Resilience among emergency medical workers was positively correlated with positive coping ( r = 0.725, p < 0.001), family support ( r = 0.621, p < 0.001), friend support ( r = 0.719, p < 0.001), other support ( r = 0.576, p < 0.001), vigor ( r = 0.730, p < 0.001), dedication ( r = 0.693, p < 0.001), and absorption ( r = 0.645, p < 0.001). Multiple linear regression analysis showed that positive coping [ β = 0.69, p = 0.001, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.30, 1.08], friend support ( β = 1.03, p = 0.039, 95% CI: 0.06, 2.01), and vigor ( β = 1.21, p = 0.002, 95% CI: 0.46, 1.96) were significantly associated with resilience. Conclusion Emergency medical team members exhibited moderately high levels of psychological resilience during the COVID-19 pandemic. Positive coping methods, support from friends, and personal vigor were significant positive associated with psychological resilience among emergency medical staff. Healthcare institutions should promote adaptive coping strategies and provide psychological support for medical staff.

title: COVID-19 vaccination uptake, safety, and clinical outcomes among patients on maintenance hemodialysis
abstract: Objectives: Patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) on maintenance hemodialysis are extremely vulnerable to severe COVID-19 infection. This prospective observational cohort study aimed to investigate the level of acceptance, determinants of hesitancy, and clinical outcomes of the COVID-19 vaccine among adult ESKD patients on regular hemodialysis in Muscat, Oman. Material and Methods: A prospective observational cohort study was conducted at a renal dialysis unit (RDU) in Muscat, Oman, between December 2020 and May 2021. The study evaluated 74 outpatients on regular hemodialysis from a total unit population of 200. Participants were included if they were ≥18 years old and on maintenance hemodialysis for ≥3 months. They were categorized based on their vaccination status at the time of follow-up. Demographic characteristics, comorbidities, dialysis vintage, vaccine side effects, COVID-19 infection rates, and mortality were analyzed. Data were collected via structured questionnaires and medical record reviews. Results: Among the 74 participants actively evaluated, 44 (60%) were willing to receive the vaccine and completed the two-dose series, while 30 (40%) refused vaccination entirely. The primary reasons for refusal included fear of side effects (43.3%), family refusal (30.1%), and cultural issues (20%). Baseline characteristics, including dialysis vintage, were similar between groups. Following the first dose, 15.9% of vaccinated patients reported adverse events, primarily fever. Across the entire RDU of 200 patients, there were 84 COVID-19 infections resulting in 10 deaths. Within the specific study cohort of 74 patients, 18 contracted COVID-19. Infection rates were 20.5% (9/44) in the vaccinated group and 30.0% (9/30) in the unvaccinated group. Using the vaccinated group as the reference, unvaccinated patients had higher odds of infection (odds ratio = 1.67, 95% confidence interval: 0.57– 4.86), though this was not statistically significant ( p = 0.413). Among the 18 infected study participants, mortality was 77.8% (7/9) in the vaccinated group and 55.6% (5/9) in the unvaccinated group ( p = 0.620). Conclusion: Vaccine hesitancy remains a significant challenge among hemodialysis patients, driven primarily by fear of adverse events and misinformation. While infection rates were numerically lower in vaccinated patients, mortality was higher among vaccinated individuals who contracted the virus, though neither finding reached statistical significance. The small sample size limits the statistical power of this study. Larger prospective studies adjusting for time-at-risk and multiple confounders are necessary to definitively determine vaccine effectiveness in this vulnerable population.

title: Sex, age and HIV-1 status influence complement activation against SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine Spike protein
abstract: Regulation of complement activity influences immunity and clinical outcomes of SARS-2 CoV-2 infections. Here we investigated antibody responses to SARS-CoV-2 vaccination and complement activity in men (age 36 to 86) and women (age 39 to 83) with (MWH, WWH) and without (MWOH, WWOH) HIV-1. Antibody responses in WWH were lower than in MWH. WWH also had negligible change in blood C3a post-immunization, whereas MWH had greater C3a levels. We investigated the levels of C5, C5a, C1-INH, factor H, and circulating immune complex-C1q (CIC-C1q) binding to understand the regulation of complement activity. We found that C1-INH and anti-S antibody levels were driving the differences in C3 convertase activity in MWH. No significant differences were found between C5 and C5a in both cohorts, suggesting that C5 convertase is not being activated. These results show that biological sex may impact SARS-CoV-2 immune responses and highlights the need for further investigation.

title: Association between prior HBV vaccine responsiveness and booster-induced anti-SARS-CoV-2 spike antibody titers following the third BNT162b2 dose in Japanese healthcare workers: A prospective observational study
abstract: Inter-individual variability in vaccine-induced humoral responses has been reported even among generally healthy individuals. In our previous study, healthcare workers with poor hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccine responsiveness were more likely to show a low anti-SARS-CoV-2 spike antibody response after the first BNT162b2 dose. This study examined whether such differences persisted after a third BNT162b2 dose. This was an extended follow-up study of a previously reported prospective observational cohort of Japanese healthcare workers. The primary outcome was the quantitative anti-SARS-CoV-2 spike antibody titer measured 12 weeks after the third BNT162b2 dose. Participants were classified as normal HBV vaccine responders, weak responders, or non-responders. Comparisons across HBV response groups were performed using the Kruskal-Wallis test and multivariable linear regression adjusted for age and sex. A low antibody-response analysis (<15 U/mL) after the first dose was evaluated as a secondary analysis. Among 741 participants with antibody measurements 12 weeks after the third dose, 486 were normal HBV vaccine responders, 229 were weak responders, and 26 were non-responders. The median anti-SARS-CoV-2 spike antibody titer was 891,900 U/mL. Titers did not differ significantly across HBV response groups in the unadjusted analysis (P = .3718) or after adjustment for age and sex (global P = .3971). Compared with normal responders, the adjusted geometric mean ratio was 0.94 (95% CI, 0.83-1.07) for weak responders and 0.83 (95% CI, 0.60-1.15) for non-responders. By contrast, after the first dose, HBV vaccine non-responders had an increased risk of a low antibody response (<15 U/mL) compared with normal responders (adjusted RR, 1.85; 95% CI, 1.10-3.13). Differences in early anti-SARS-CoV-2 spike antibody responses associated with prior HBV vaccine responsiveness were no longer statistically apparent 12 weeks after the third BNT162b2 dose. These findings suggest convergence of measured humoral antibody responses after booster vaccination, although they do not establish that the underlying biological mechanisms of vaccine hyporesponsiveness were eliminated.

title: SARS-CoV-2 Nsp2 reprograms host immunity to drive pathogenic inflammation
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite the end of the COVID-19 pandemic, SARS-CoV-2 continues to circulate endemically, highlighting the need to better understand the viral determinants of pathogenesis. Putative functions of the non-structural protein 2 (Nsp2) have been studied in vitro , but how Nsp2 affects pathogenesis and overall viral fitness in vivo has yet to be demonstrated. Here, we generated a recombinant SARS-CoV-2 lacking Nsp2 (ΔNsp2) to investigate its role in viral replication and disease. While ΔNsp2 replicated comparably to wild-type virus in vitro and in vivo , its deletion resulted in markedly attenuated disease in K18-hACE2 mice. Wild-type virus infection induced a strong pro-inflammatory response associated with increased recruitment of monocytes and macrophages, whereas ΔNsp2 virus infection promoted a more balanced antiviral response characterized by enhanced lymphocyte and NK cell recruitment. This was accompanied by reduced pulmonary and systemic inflammation and distinct transcriptional programs, including downregulation of pathways related to RNA processing and translation. Mechanistically, CLIP-seq and proximity labeling suggest that Nsp2 interacts with host RNA and components of the translational machinery. Together, our findings identify Nsp2 as a key virulence factor that drives immunopathology by skewing host immune responses, highlighting its role as a regulator of host–pathogen interactions. IMPORTANCE The COVID-19 pandemic has officially ended, yet the virus that causes it continues to circulate and evolve, making it important to understand what makes it cause severe disease. This study focuses on a viral protein called Nsp2 and asks what role it plays in driving illness. Using an animal model, we observed that when Nsp2 was removed from the virus, infected animals became far less sick, even though the virus itself replicated just as well. Instead of triggering the harmful, excessive inflammation typically seen with the full virus, the modified virus prompted a more balanced immune response. Further investigation revealed that Nsp2 interacts directly with the host’s genetic machinery, suggesting a mechanism by which the virus hijacks immune signaling to worsen disease. These findings pinpoint Nsp2 as a driver of COVID-19 severity and a promising target for future therapies aimed at reducing inflammation rather than simply fighting the virus itself.

title: Living with SARS-CoV-2: A 6-year reflection on the pandemic’s ongoing impact and future implications
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic seems to be something of the past, but the virus is still here and causing disease. We are not genuinely back to "normal." Are we taking the right actions to protect our populations? The evidence on SARS-CoV-2 reveals concerning information. The virus mutates at a high rate, giving rise to new variants infecting large parts of our populations several times a year. While acute illness is generally less severe today, we cannot be certain that future variants will have a similar virulence. In addition, the long-term sequelae observed in many organ systems suggest severe consequences, of which we have not yet seen the full magnitude. This article discusses coping mechanisms that may explain the disconnect between our knowledge and public health actions. It calls for multidisciplinary collaboration to identify sustainable and responsible ways to live with SARS-CoV-2.

source_records.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic seems to be something of the past, but the virus is still here and causing disease. We are not genuinely back to "normal." Are we taking the right actions to protect our populations? The evidence on SARS-CoV-2 reveals concerning information. The virus mutates at a high rate, giving rise to new variants infecting large parts of our populations several times a year. While acute illness is generally less severe today, we cannot be certain that future variants will have a similar virulence. In addition, the long-term sequelae observed in many organ systems suggest severe consequences, of which we have not yet seen the full magnitude. This article discusses coping mechanisms that may explain the disconnect between our knowledge and public health actions. It calls for multidisciplinary collaboration to identify sustainable and responsible ways to live with SARS-CoV-2.

title: Lessons learned from predicting hospital admission criteria comparing two COVID-19 waves: an emergency department's perspective.
abstract: Methods This study compares patient characteristics, clinical biomarkers and outcomes during wave 1 (W1) and wave 2 (W2) of the COVID-19 pandemic at two tertiary care EDs in Berlin. We validated parameters predicting hospital admission by a CART-analysis of W1 in W2 and compared the findings to a CART-model derived from W2 by a decision curve analysis. Results A total of 1204 patients with suspected COVID-19 presented in W1 and 1,440 in W2; 106 in W1 and 722 in W2 tested positive. Patients in W2 were older (>65 years, W1: 22.2%; W2: 34.6%) and multimorbid. Mortality of positive tested (W1: 1.9%; W2:8.6%) rose in W2. The admission-predicting parameters O2 saturation Conclusions Our results show transferability of admission-criteria despite changing pandemic conditions and serve as lessons learned to support future pandemic preparedness and capacity planning.

title: Cellular origin and characterization of autoantibodies against type I IFNs in COVID-19 and APS-1.
abstract: Autoantibodies against type I IFNs can severely compromise antiviral defense, yet the mechanisms underlying their development remain elusive. Using high-throughput autoantigen profiling, we observed that a subgroup of severe COVID-19 patients exhibited strong binding to multiple type I IFNs. Integrated single-cell RNA and B cell receptor (BCR) sequencing with functional analysis identified B cell subsets/states enriched for IFN-α2-binding and -neutralizing antibodies in COVID-19. These findings were compared with those from patients with autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type I, a rare genetic disease characterized by defective immune tolerance and persistent type I IFN autoimmunity. Competition surface plasmon resonance and AlphaFold 3 structural modeling identified three major functional epitope groups and seven predicted structural subclasses among neutralizing antibodies. Our results indicate that IFN-α2 autoreactivity is present in both naive and antigen-experienced B cell compartments, whereas functional IFN-neutralizing antibodies are predominantly associated with memory and atypical B cells, consistent with defective tolerance and affinity maturation-mediated selection of autoreactive B cell clones.

title: Association between obstructive sleep apnea severity and clinical outcomes in COVID-19 patients: a retrospective study
abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) may influence the clinical course of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). This study aimed first to determine the prevalence of COVID-19 among patients with polysomnography-confirmed OSA and subsequently to evaluate the association between OSA severity and clinical outcomes in patients with COVID-19. Patients diagnosed with OSA or simple snoring by polysomnography were screened through the hospital database for COVID-19. Demographic and clinical characteristics, hospitalization, mortality, and laboratory parameters were analyzed. Among 431 patients with OSA, 183 (42%) were diagnosed with COVID-19, and complete clinical data were available for 79 patients. The study included 181 patients: 79 with OSA and 102 age-matched controls. Admission peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) and length of hospital stay differed significantly across OSA severity groups ( p < 0.05). Among patients with OSA, those with severe OSA had higher rates of dyspnea and nasal oxygen requirement at admission. In unadjusted analyses, the apnea–hypopnea index (AHI) was positively correlated with length of hospital stay, lactate dehydrogenase, fibrinogen, and C-reactive protein levels and negatively correlated with admission SpO2. In the multivariable linear regression model, fibrinogen was significantly associated with ln(AHI) (B = 0.00187, p = 0.011), whereas hypertension was not significantly associated ( p = 0.169). In the ordinal logistic regression model, smoking, platelet count, and mean platelet volume were significantly associated with higher ordered study-group categories. These findings indicate that although greater OSA severity was associated with several markers of a more complicated COVID-19 course in unadjusted analyses, many of these associations were attenuated after multivariable adjustment. Further studies with larger cohorts and more complete assessment of potential confounders are needed to clarify the independent contribution of OSA severity to COVID-19 outcomes. Clinical trial number: Not applicable.

title: Global return-on-investment of COVID-19 vaccines in the first year of the vaccination programme: A model-based economic evaluation
abstract: BACKGROUND: COVID-19 vaccines played a critical role in reducing global health burden during the COVID-19 pandemic, but their rapid development required extraordinary effort. This study aims to evaluate their global return-on-investment (ROI) during the first year of the vaccination programme (8 December 2020-8 December 2021) to provide insights into the economic benefits relative to the costs of vaccine development, manufacturing, and delivery. METHODS AND FINDINGS: Public health outcomes of COVID-19 vaccination, including life years and quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) gained from averted deaths, infections, and hospitalizations, were estimated. Health benefits were valued using two approaches: i) cost-benefit analysis and ii) cost-effectiveness analysis. These benefits were compared to the costs of vaccine development, manufacturing, and delivery to estimate the ROI under both approaches. Probabilistic sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the impact of parameter uncertainty on ROI estimates. Vaccine development and delivery cost $79.4 billion, but the health and economic benefits of vaccination were valued between $6.43 and $64.3 trillion. High-income countries saw the greatest health benefits per-person vaccinated, and low-income countries gained the greatest nonhealth benefits per-person vaccinated, when expressed as a proportion of gross domestic product per capita. This estimated ROIs of $59.7-$809 per dollar invested in the base case analysis. ROIs ranged between $60.3-$753 across probabilistic sensitivity analyses for both approaches. Limitations include reliance on previous analyses of COVID-19 vaccination impact and a time horizon limited to the first year of COVID-19 vaccination. CONCLUSIONS: Rapid COVID-19 vaccine development and delivery were an excellent investment. Vaccine development and equitable vaccine distribution globally should be prioritized before and during global health crises.

title: Lecciones de las pandemias de influenza y de COVID-19 para la odontología: revisión sistemática Lessons from influenza and COVID-19 pandemics for dentistry: a systematic review
abstract: Objetivo: sintetizar las lecciones de los brotes históricos de influenza y de la pandemia de COVID-19 aplicables a la atención odontológica. Método: revisión sistemática con síntesis narrativa en PubMed y SciELO (2012-2025); se incluyeron 15 estudios: revisiones sistemáticas y narrativas, ensayos clínicos y documentos de análisis histórico. Resultados: la pandemia de 1918 mostró el valor de proteger al personal sanitario y la de 2009, el de los diagnósticos moleculares y del uso planificado de los antivirales. En odontología, la COVID-19 obligó a controlar los aerosoles, reforzar la bioseguridad, priorizar la atención urgente, evaluar colutorios antisépticos y atender el agotamiento profesional. Conclusión: la preparación odontológica exige protocolos permanentes de bioseguridad y planes de continuidad asistencial.

title: Assessment of coronavirus disease 2019 mRNA vaccine response in kidney transplant recipients
abstract: Kidney transplant recipients are vulnerable to developing severe coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) infection. Although mRNA vaccines have significantly improved outcomes, seropositivity rates remain variable in immunosuppressed patients. This study aimed to evaluate the antibody response to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, identify factors affecting immunogenicity, and examine the association between antibody titers and subsequent SARS-CoV-2 infection and COVID-19-related hospitalization among kidney transplant recipients. We retrospectively studied 372 adult kidney transplant recipients who received two doses of COVID-19 mRNA vaccine after transplantation and had anti-SARS‐CoV‐2 spike protein receptor-binding domain antibodies measured ≥ 14 days after the second dose and prior to receiving a third dose. We categorized patients based on previous COVID-19 infection, post-vaccination antibody status (seropositive or seronegative), and antibody titers (low or high). Factors associated with poor vaccine response (seronegativity) and with high antibody titers (antibody titer ≥ 121 U/mL) were determined using multivariable regression models. The proportion of patients with subsequent COVID-19 infection was higher in the seronegative group than in the seropositive or previous infection groups (36% vs. 13%, respectively; P = 0.02). Multivariable regression analysis revealed higher odds of poor response to the mRNA vaccine among patients aged > 52 years compared with those aged ≤ 52 years (aOR = 1.94; 95% CI: 1.12-3.36; P = 0.018). Lower odds were observed among male patients (aOR = 0.43; 95% CI: 0.24-0.77; P = 0.004) and those taking azathioprine (aOR = 0.26; 95% CI: 0.07-0.91; P = 0.035). The proportion of patients with subsequent COVID-19 was also higher in the low-antibody group than in the high-antibody group (33% vs. Multivariable logistic regression analysis showed lower odds of high SARS-CoV-2 antibody titers among patients aged > 51 years compared with those aged ≤ 51 years (aOR = 0.43; 95% CI: 0.24-0.75; P = 0.003). Higher odds were observed among those of African race (aOR = 2.82; 95% CI: 1.11-7.16; P = 0.03) and South Asian race (aOR = 2.27; 95% CI: 1.08-4.75; P = 0.03) compared with Middle Eastern recipients. Understanding the immunologic response to the SARS-CoV-2 vaccine in kidney transplant recipients is essential for preventing potentially life-threatening infection. Furthermore, identifying transplant recipients with a low vaccine-induced antibody response may help guide the development of individualized immunization strategies.

title: eNAMPT is a plasma biomarker of COVID-19 severity and ARDS progression linked to increased immune effector cell expression
abstract: BACKGROUND: The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the critical unmet need for novel targets, biomarkers, and effective pharmacotherapies to reduce the severity/mortality of COVID pneumonia and progression to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Extracellular NAMPT (eNAMPT) is a druggable DAMP and TLR4 ligand centrally involved in ARDS pathobiology. We explored the utility of plasma eNAMPT measurements as a potential COVID-19 biomarker linked to ARDS progression and disease severity and investigated the potential cellular source for eNAMPT release/secretion in COVID-19 subjects. METHODS: A plasma biomarker panel of inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-1RA, TNF-α), DAMPs (eNAMPT, MIF) and vascular proteins (ANG-2, PSGL-1) were evaluated in three distinct COVID-19-positive cohorts (Miami, Arizona, Tampa) (n = 277) and healthy control subjects (n = 214). Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) publicly available on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) in a subset of Tampa COVID-19 survivors (n = 18) and an autopsied COVID lung tissue database was separately analyzed for biomarker gene expression. RESULTS: Plasma biomarkers, including eNAMPT were significantly elevated in COVID-19 subjects compared to healthy controls (p < 0.0001), with IL-1RA, IL-6 and eNAMPT exhibiting the strongest diagnostic performance. Biomarker levels (all except IL-8, MIF) were higher in COVID-19 ARDS cases vs COVID-19 pneumonia (n = 154, AUC 0.71-0.79, p < 0.05) and were significantly elevated in COVID non-survivors (IL-6, IL-1RA, TNF-α, eNAMPT, ANG-2, PSGL-1) compared to survivors (p < 0.05). NAMPT gene expression was significantly upregulated in COVID-19 PBMCs compared with healthy controls, most evident within the CD14 + monocyte cluster. Relative to lung tissue from non-COVID-19 infected, NAMPT gene expression was increased in specific COVID-19 lung cell populations, including neutrophils, CD16 + monocytes, conventional dendritic cells (cDCs), fibroblasts, endothelium, and alveolar macrophages. CONCLUSION: Our study corroborated the utility of this biomarker panel for diagnostic and severity assessment in COVID-19- associated ARDS and as a strategy for subject stratification in therapeutic trials of eNAMPT-neutralizing therapies. We further identified NAMPT expression in immune effector cells that correlates with COVID-19 severity and lethality. Together, these findings suggest NAMPT plays a key role in sustaining inflammatory activation and impairing lung regeneration in fatal COVID-19.

title: Persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection in SCID rats reflects immune vulnerability of the upper airway and trachea
abstract: ABSTRACT In immunocompromised patients, persistent severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection carries the risk of prolonged viral shedding and emergence of new variants. To reproduce the key features of persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection and evaluate its transmissibility, mouse-passaged SARS-CoV-2 was administered intranasally to severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) rats deficient in Rag2 and Il2rg genes. The virus replicated in SCID rats for at least 6 weeks without causing severe symptoms. The main replication sites were the nasal cavity and trachea, and replicating viruses were barely detectable in the lungs. Infected areas within the nasal cavity and trachea showed minimal infiltration of neutrophils and M2 macrophages; however, a strong inflammatory response was observed in the lungs. Serial sequencing of the viral genome revealed accumulation of persistent mutations, predominantly in regions encoding nonstructural proteins. The persistently shed virus retained its infectivity, enabling its transmission to uninfected SCID rats. This model provides new insights into the immunological and tissue-associated features of persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection and offers a practical research platform for developing therapeutic interventions. IMPORTANCE Persistent severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection in immunocompromised individuals promotes viral evolution and ongoing transmission, yet mechanistic studies have been limited by the absence of appropriate animal models. Existing mouse systems do not support longitudinal sampling or evaluate transmission, leaving critical questions unanswered. We established an SCID rat model that enables repeated noninvasive sampling from the same individuals, allowing longitudinal analysis of viral dynamics during prolonged infection. This approach revealed the emergence, disappearance, and fixation of viral mutations over time. Persistently infected rats also retained infectious and transmitted virus to naïve SCID rats, providing experimental evidence that prolonged infection preserves the transmission potential in this model. Persistent viral replication localized to the nasal cavity and trachea may be relevant to the upper-airway persistence reported in some immunocompromised patients. By capturing selected features of persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection under profoundly immunodeficient conditions, this model provides a valuable platform for investigating viral persistence, evolution, and transmission.

title: Neuroinflammation as a Mechanism in Long COVID
abstract: Long COVID is recognized as a chronic post-viral condition characterized by fatigue, cognitive impairment, mood changes, and other neuropsychiatric symptoms that go beyond the acute phase of COVID-19. More research is now suggesting that neuroinflammation processes, involving microglial reactivity, altered cytokine signaling, and increased permeability of the blood-brain barrier, may contribute to the persistence of these symptoms. This paper provides a critical review of four recent empirical studies that directly examined neuroinflammatory mechanisms in individuals with long COVID using functional neuroimaging, biomarker analysis, and structural MRI measures. Across studies, converging evidence shows persistent central and peripheral immune activation linked to deficits in memory, attention, and mood regulation. Despite promising findings, the literature is limited by small sample sizes, inconsistent diagnostic criteria, and primarily cross-sectional designs, which limit conclusions about causality. Differences in imaging techniques and biomarker measurement approaches hinder direct comparison and synthesis of results. Future research should prioritize longitudinal, multimodal designs that integrate neuroimaging with immune and behavioral markers to clarify the trajectory and clinical relevance of neuroinflammation in long COVID. Overall, the evidence suggests that neuroinflammation plays a significant role in long COVID related cognitive and mood disturbances and emphasizes the need for biologically guided and consistent clinical approaches.
journal: Journal of Clinical Psychology and Neurology

title: Comparative analysis of the development of oral language as a cognitive process constitutive of learning in child cohorts exposed to COVID-19 lockdown
abstract: This study analyzes oral language development as a constitutive cognitive process of learning in child cohorts exposed to COVID-19 confinement. A mixed-method, comparative, and correlational approach is proposed with a sample of 60 children distributed across three cohorts: pre-, during-, and post-pandemic. Exposure to the pandemic context is examined through questionnaires and interviews with parents and caregivers, while language development is assessed through PLON-R, systematic observation, and pedagogical records. The theoretical review and available contextual evidence suggest variations in morphosyntactic, semantic, and pragmatic performance associated with reduced social interaction, disrupted routines, and lower communicative stimulation. The study provides an analytical basis for understanding the relationship among confinement, language, and learning, and for supporting educational and psychopedagogical interventions in post-pandemic contexts.
journal: Journal of Systems and Educational Management

title: Autopsy findings after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination: a German national registry study
abstract: Abstract Autopsies are the foundation of evidence-based medicine and gold standard for determining causes of death. A potential causal relationship between COVID-19 vaccination and death remains a subject of debate, however multidisciplinary, multicentric national autopsy studies are missing. N = 486 eligible SARS-CoV-2 vaccinated autopsy cases from 14 German pathology, neuropathology and legal medicine university centres between 2021 and 2024 were available via the German National Autopsy Registry. For comparison COVID-19 autopsies were included ( n = 385 cases, all performed before the vaccination campaign in Germany started). A previously established causality algorithm was applied in a consensus assessment of potential causality between vaccine administration and an adverse event following immunization (AEFI). N = 176 cases with a post vaccination interval ≤ 28d were included into analyses. In a single case of allergic reaction, in 5/8 cases of either myocarditis ( n = 4 cases) or perimyocarditis ( n = 1 case), and 9/26 cases of thromboembolism, the consensus process resulted in a potential AEFI in these cases, but no definite causality. In n = 3 cases in which the cause of death remained unclear after autopsy, no potential AEFI could be established. In SARS-CoV-2 positive autopsy cases without vaccination, thromboembolism was documented as cause of death in 18/385 cases and myocarditis in 2/385 cases. In conclusion, autopsies are a valuable tool to assess adverse effects. Currently, post vaccination autopsy numbers are too low to draw conclusions on the general population or to identify rare AEFI signals. As part of pandemic preparedness, international guidelines for post vaccination autopsy procedures, diagnostics and interpretation are necessary. Autopsy registries can support this collective effort.

journal: Archiv für Pathologische Anatomie und Physiologie und für Klinische Medicin

title: Occupational Preparedness Among Peruvian Police Officers: Exploratory Institutional Comparisons With Army Personnel During the COVID-19 Pandemic
abstract: Abstract Objective Non-health care first responders are essential components of public health emergency response systems, yet their occupational preparedness during health crises remains insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to describe occupational conditions before and during the COVID-19 pandemic among Peruvian police officers and Army personnel and explore institutional differences in preparedness-related characteristics. Methods A secondary cross-sectional analysis was conducted using survey data from 512 active-duty personnel in Peru, including 352 police officers and 160 Army personnel. Occupational conditions before and during the pandemic were described, including work organization, transportation, training, perceived preparedness, mistreatment, and self-procurement of protective supplies. Exploratory unadjusted comparisons were performed using chi-square tests. Results During the pandemic, participants reported increased public-order assignments (26.9% vs. 18.3%), field-based work (40.3% vs. 36.0%), walking commuting (62.1% vs. 37.9%), and longer commuting times. Although 72.9% reported face-to-face COVID-19 training, 88.1% did not feel qualified to address COVID-19-related issues. Masks were self-purchased by 60.5% of participants. Institutional differences were observed in COVID-19-related health status, occupation type, and perceived preparedness. Conclusions Preparedness among security forces during public health emergencies requires more than training delivery. Emergency plans should incorporate tailored education, risk communication, protective supply planning, and institutional support for non-health care first responders.

title: Preliminary evaluation of qualitative RT-PCR and indirect immunofluorescence for SARS-CoV-2 detection in nasopharyngeal swabs samples
abstract: Introduction: The COVID-19 pandemic made it essential to expand SARS-CoV-2 diagnostic capacity. Two laboratory techniques—qualitative RT-PCR and indirect immunofluorescence (IIF)—were preliminarily evaluated for virus detection in nasopharyngeal samples. Methods: RNA extracted from nasopharyngeal swabs of patients with infection confirmed by RT-qPCR was used to establish the amplification conditions for a 128-bp fragment of the SARS-CoV-2 N gene by RT-PCR. Under the selected conditions, 65 samples from patients with clinical manifestations compatible with COVID-19 were analyzed. For IIF, a purified preparation of anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibodies obtained from positive serum samples previously analyzed with a commercial ELISA was used. The antibodies bound to viral antigens in cells from nasopharyngeal swabs and were detected with a fluorescein isothiocyanate-conjugated anti-human IgG antibody. Results: The selected conditions for amplification of the 128-bp fragment were 1.5 mM MgCl2, 0.6 μM of each primer, 0.2 mM dNTPs, 5.0 U of Taq polymerase and 5.0 U of reverse transcriptase, and an annealing temperature of 57 °C. Under these conditions, 64 of 65 samples (98.46%) yielded the expected amplicon. IIF revealed fluorescence-positive cells and showed no reactivity against the evaluated panel of other viruses. Conclusion: Qualitative RT-PCR and IIF showed favorable preliminary results for SARS-CoV-2 detection in nasopharyngeal samples. A complete analytical and clinical evaluation is required before either technique can be considered for diagnostic use.

title: Factors influencing COVID-19 vaccination among adolescents in Western Mexico: the role of family influence and access barriers
abstract: Background and purpose COVID-19 vaccination remains an important public health strategy. Adolescents represent approximately 16% of the global population (1.3 billion), making their vaccine uptake a critical component of pandemic control. This study aimed to identify the factors and barriers influencing COVID-19 vaccination behaviors among adolescents in western Mexico. Methods A non-experimental, observational, cross-sectional study was conducted in high school students aged 15–17 years. Data were collected through an online Google Forms questionnaire. Statistical analysis included chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests and binary logistic regression to evaluate factors associated with vaccination behavior. Results A total of 838 adolescents were included, of whom 83% received at least one dose of the COVID-19 vaccine. Sociodemographic characteristics including age, sex, and religion, were not significantly associated with vaccination attitudes. In contrast, parental influence, particularly maternal attitudes and vaccination behaviors, showed a stronger association with adolescent vaccination status than paternal attitudes. Additionally, parental refusal, family dynamics, and structural accessibility barriers had a greater influence on vaccine hesitancy than concerns regarding vaccine safety or effectiveness among adolescents in western Mexico. Conclusion These findings highlight the need for public health strategies that address access barriers and family-centered approaches when evaluating adolescent vaccination behaviors. Interventions focused solely on correcting misinformation are unlikely to be sufficient without addressing these broader factors.

title: Giám sát SARS-CoV-2 trong nước thải tại Hà Nội giai đoạn 2021–2024: Áp dụng hệ thống giám sát môi trường vi rút bại liệt
abstract: Giám sát môi trường nước thải (Wastewater and Environmental Surveillance – WES) ngày càng được quantâm như một công cụ bổ sung cho giám sát bệnh truyền nhiễm. Tại Việt Nam, WES đã được áp dụng để pháthiện SARS-CoV-2 trong nước thải, nhưng chủ yếu ở quy mô nhỏ và tại một số khu vực. Nghiên cứu mô tả hồicứu sử dụng 145 mẫu nước thải được thu thập từ hệ thống giám sát môi trường vi rút bại liệt tại Hà Nội tronggiai đoạn 2021–2024. Mẫu được xét nghiệm SARS-CoV-2 bằng kỹ thuật real-time RT-PCR nhắm đích gen E,với ngưỡng Ct ≤ 38. Trong tổng số 145 mẫu, 42 mẫu dương tính với SARS-CoV-2, tương ứng tỷ lệ phát hiệnchung là 29,0%. Tỷ lệ phát hiện tại các điểm giám sát dao động từ 16,3% đến 39,5% và không khác biệt có ýnghĩa thống kê giữa nhóm cống gom nước thải và nhóm trạm xử lý nước thải (p = 0,5903). Không ghi nhậnmẫu dương tính trong năm 2021; tỷ lệ phát hiện cao nhất vào năm 2022 (56,1%), sau đó giảm còn 26,3% năm2023 và 18,2% năm 2024. Xu hướng phát hiện SARS-CoV-2 trong nước thải nhìn chung song hành với diễnbiến dịch COVID-19 tại Việt Nam. Kết quả cho thấy WES có thể cung cấp thông tin bổ sung về sự lưu hành củaSARS-CoV-2 trong cộng đồng và góp phần tăng cường năng lực giám sát bệnh truyền nhiễm theo cách tiếpcận Một sức khỏe tại Việt Nam.

title: Utilization of the Nortropinone Scaffold in the Structure-Guided Design of Potent Inhibitors of Human Cathepsin L and the Chymotrypsin-like Proteases of SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV
abstract: Abstract Coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV, encode two large polyproteins, pp1a and pp1ab, that are primarily processed by highly conserved 3C-like proteases, yielding an array of structural and nonstructural proteins essential for viral replication. SARS-CoV-2 3CLpro is deemed to be a well-established and validated antiviral target. During cell entry, pathogenic coronaviruses, particularly the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variants, utilize host cell cathepsins, including cathepsin L (CatL), and the endosomal pathway for successful infection. Furthermore, SARS-CoV-2 infection results in overexpression of CatL, which, in turn, intensifies SARS-CoV-2 infection. Consequently, CatL has emerged as a potential target for the development of COVID-19 therapeutics. We report herein a series of inhibitors that incorporate in their structure a nortropinone scaffold as a design element for probing and exploiting poorly explored regions of chemical space. The inhibitors were found to be noncytotoxic and to potently inhibit CatL and the 3CLpro of MERS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2. The IC50 values of compound 12 against human CatL, MERS-CoV 3CLpro, and SARS-CoV-2 3CLpro were determined to be 0.12 nM, 0.11 μM, and 0.38 μM, respectively. Furthermore, compound 12 was found to inhibit SARS-CoV-2 infection in vitro with an EC50 value of 0.09 ± 0.05 μM and a Safety Index >1100. High-resolution cocrystal structures with SARS-CoV-2 3CLpro and MERS-CoV 3CLpro confirmed the mechanism of action of the compounds, illuminated the molecular determinants associated with binding, and informed the optimization of the inhibitors.

title: Epidemiología del SARS-CoV-2 en la práctica odontológica: transmisión, carga viral salival y bioseguridad Epidemiology of SARS-CoV-2 in dental practice: transmission, salivary viral load and biosafety
abstract: Objetivo: sintetizar la evidencia sobre la transmisión del SARS-CoV-2 en la práctica odontológica, la carga viral salival y las medidas de bioseguridad. Método: revisión sistemática con síntesis narrativa en PubMed y SciELO (2012-2025); se incluyeron 15 estudios. Resultados: la saliva y los aerosoles de los procedimientos odontológicos son vías relevantes de transmisión. La detección molecular del virus en saliva respalda su papel como reservorio y como muestra diagnóstica. Los colutorios antisépticos reducen el virus in vitro, pero su efecto clínico sobre la carga viral salival es limitado. El triaje, la protección personal, el control de aerosoles y la teleodontología fueron las medidas centrales. Conclusión: la bioseguridad debe mantenerse como norma permanente.

title: Pulmonary vascular abnormalities in Long COVID: a radiological perspective
abstract: Post-COVID-19 condition (Long COVID) has emerged as a major public health challenge, with survivors frequently reporting persistent dyspnea, fatigue, and exercise intolerance. While initial radiological research focused on parenchymal lung disease, a paradigm shift has identified pulmonary vascular abnormalities—specifically endotheliitis, microthrombosis, and maladaptive angiogenesis—as critical drivers of the Long COVID phenotype. The disease is characterized by “endotheliitis,” where direct viral entry via ACE2 receptors precipitates a pro-coagulant state and the formation of in situ microthrombi. This is further complicated by immunothrombosis involving neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) and the presence of amyloid-like fibrin microclots that are resistant to natural breakdown. Additionally, structural remodeling through intussusceptive angiogenesis and “vascular pruning” (the loss of distal capillaries) reduces the effective surface area for gas exchange. Conventional CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) often fails to detect these microvascular changes, despite patients exhibiting severe symptoms. However, advanced modalities provide deeper insights. Dual-energy CT (DECT) reveals persistent, wedge-shaped perfusion defects even in morphologically normal lung parenchyma. Quantitative CT (QCT) allows for the measurement of “vascular pruning,” showing a significant reduction in small vessel volume (PBV5). Hyperpolarized xenon-129 MRI (Hp-XeMRI) has identified a hallmark Red blood cell (RBC):barrier defect, indicating impaired gas transfer from the alveoli to red blood cells—a finding that persists even when standard CT and pulmonary function tests are normal. Functional techniques like V/Q SPECT and phase-resolved functional lung (PREFUL) MRI further confirm a “mottled” perfusion pattern indicative of diffuse small vessel vasculopathy. This review emphasizes that Long COVID involves a distinct vascular phenotype that requires functional and quantitative imaging for accurate diagnosis. Adherence to the 2025 international consensus guidelines—recommending imaging 3 months post-infection and the use of paired inspiratory/expiratory protocols—is essential for standardizing care and differentiating vascular from airway-related symptoms.
